doc.title: Jason Palmer interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 2, 2025

title: Teaching ensembles at Berklee with historical listening sessions
summary: Palmer coaches mid-level Berklee ensembles, brings in songs with stories, hosts listening sessions and interviews students at semester start.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: How do you find time to work that into your lessons?

You know it depends on the student. You know at Berklee I teach in the ensemble department so a lot of times I’m coaching ensembles and so what I do is when I bring in repertoire, I try to bring in songs that have stories behind them or some kind of historical reference or whatnot. And I try to take at least a week where we’ll go maybe have pizza or I’ll host a recording session — not recording — a listening session where I’ll play recordings, historical recordings, and we’ll just talk outside of class time. And I usually do that towards the end of the semester, especially for the students who — my role at Berklee is I work in the Ensemble Department and there they have certain levels for all the ensembles in order for all the students to be hopefully placed in groups where they all have the same or similar level of playing and experience. And so I’m dealing with levels 3s, 4s, and 5s, which is the mid-level. 6, 7, 8 are the upper levels. So I’m dealing with a lot of students who are pretty new to the music. They may not know who all the great players are. So I tend to spend a little more time, you know, bringing in historical recordings and even some recordings and charts of our contemporaries that are really writing music that has a really strong steep in the tradition but also, you know, trying to find new things within compositional practices and everything. So I try to do a mix, and

you know it all varies from ensemble to ensemble. You know some ensembles I’ll get where a lot of the students want to play straight ahead and then I have some ensembles where they want to, you know, learn the modern thing and play songs from contemporaries. So what I do in the beginning of the semester is always interview the students in the ensembles. I’ll ask okay what have you been listening to, how long have you been playing, you know did you grow up in a musical family. And so what that does is it kind of informs me as to what they like and what I think could help them get to the next level. You know, so based on what they already know and where their skill level is then I’ll just bring in things that I think will really augment their time, you know, with me in the semester.
